top.line: Anyone can fork, so every corner is protected
top.para: Founders, customers and investors are each protected from the others because anyone can fork, given no broad non-compete and portable data. Forks take hold only after a breakdown such as a licence change or new owner; where the original keeps executing, as MySQL did, the fork stays a hedge. Real limits remain.

in-short.line: Forks win after breakdowns; execution is the defence
in-short.para: Only 7 of 220 significant forks merged back. LibreOffice, io.js, Nextcloud, OpenTofu and Valkey each followed a new owner, governance fight or licence change, while MariaDB never caught MySQL, whose commits have since fallen by about two thirds. The best investors depend on the code, and bigger players, brands and costs limit the protection.

triangle.line: Each corner has an exit, with a condition attached
triangle.para: In an open source company customers stay for service and trust, not access. If founders stop executing, investors fund a team next door; if investors change direction, founders leave with the code; if anyone fails customers, they move. Each exit needs money, no broad non-compete, or portable data.

breaks.line: Famous forks followed a breakdown, not a slowdown
breaks.para: Robles and González-Barahona found only 7 of 220 forks merged back and 30% outlived a discontinued original. LibreOffice followed Oracle's purchase of Sun, io.js a governance fight then reunion, OpenTofu Terraform's BSL change, and Valkey the Redis licence change eight days earlier. Each original stopped doing what users needed.

executing.line: While the original executes, a fork stays a hedge
executing.para: MariaDB never displaced MySQL, now second in DB-Engines against MariaDB's thirteenth. MySQL's commits fell from about 8,900 in 2019 to about 2,800 in 2025, so MariaDB should now grow, a checkable prediction. The real defence is execution and speed: a competitor who forks gets your position, not your velocity.

investors.line: Investors who depend on the code back forks fastest
investors.para: Valkey's backers ran managed Redis services and OpenTofu's ran products on Terraform, so they funded alternatives quickly without needing control. Chemmanur, Loutskina and Tian found corporate-backed startups produced 26.9% more patents with 17.6% more citations. That such investors earn better returns is my guess, without data.

founders.line: Founders can fork away only without broad non-competes
founders.para: Frank Karlitschek left ownCloud in 2016 and launched Nextcloud on a fork, profitable by the end of that year. Venture deals usually demand non-competes, as the NVCA model shows, and shareholder covenants face lighter legal limits. Founders should refuse broad non-competes and offer confidentiality, non-poaching and brand promises instead.

customers.line: Open code is not enough; customers need portable data
customers.para: When ownCloud's US company closed, Nextcloud offered its customers free transition support, and moving was cheap because the data stayed on their own servers. A customer's real exit is their data in an open format, movable at near zero cost, so a company claiming customers stay for service should make leaving easy.

maturity.line: Maturity is fine; open source frees the explorers
maturity.para: Companies become town planners in Wardley's sense, and that is healthy, but closed companies trap explorers' ideas. Open source offers a neutral home, as Google gave Kubernetes to the CNCF in 2015 to make it the standard across clouds, and lets explorers take the code and carry on elsewhere.

care.line: Bigger players, surviving brands and costs limit forks
care.para: Redis and Elastic were out-served by cloud providers selling their healthy code. Redis remains far above Valkey in DB-Engines, and both later restored open licences under fork pressure. OpenTofu needed 18 developers for five years, so the threat suits dependent investors, and single copyright holders can still change future terms.

limits.line: The cases fit the argument but prove nothing
limits.para: No study tests the triangle as a whole, famous forks bring survivorship bias, and higher returns for open source investors are a guess. Commit counts are rough, non-compete law varies, not every component belongs in a foundation, and my own companies run on open source, so I have a stake.

sources.line: Sources: fork studies, foundations, licences and investor research
sources.para: The piece began as my voice memo of 16 October 2026, with MySQL commits counted from a clone of mysql/mysql-server. Sources include Robles and González-Barahona's fork study, The Document Foundation, the Linux Foundation on OpenTofu and Valkey, DB-Engines, Redis and Elastic licensing notes, Chemmanur, Loutskina and Tian, Nextcloud, the NVCA and Wardley.
